explanations.answer: Ahab goes disguised and Jehoshaphat wears royal robes
explanations.explanation: That's the plan. Ahab, king of Israel, says, "I will disguise myself and go into battle, but you wear your royal robes." Jehoshaphat is king of Judah, so he's the one dressed like a king. I think his closet was about to get way more attention than he ever wanted.

explanations.answer: Both kings go into battle in disguise
explanations.explanation: Close, but only one king is hiding. Ahab says, "I will disguise myself," and then he turns to Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, and tells him to wear his royal robes. So one king is in disguise and the other is dressed as himself. Two disguises would be a whole different battle.

explanations.answer: Both kings go into battle in royal robes
explanations.explanation: Only one king keeps the robes on. Ahab, king of Israel, says, "I will disguise myself and go into battle." It's Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, who is told, "…you wear your royal robes." So the two kings walk in dressed very differently.

Israel is right. The king of Aram orders his thirty-two chariot commanders, "Do not fight with anyone, small or great, except the king of Israel." That's a short list of one. Every commander knows exactly who he's looking for.

Judah is where Jehoshaphat is king, and he's fighting right next to Ahab. But the order doesn't name him. It says, "…except the king of Israel." Ahab is the king of Israel, so he's the one on the list.

Edom doesn't show up in this order at all. The king of Aram tells his chariot commanders not to fight with anyone, small or great, "except the king of Israel." That's the only name on his list. Easy to remember: one king, one target.

True. The chariot commanders see Jehoshaphat in his royal robes and say, "Surely this is the king of Israel!" Then they turn to fight against him. They're doing what their king ordered, and the robes sure make it look like they found their man.

Actually, they do make that call. The text says the chariot commanders saw Jehoshaphat and said, "Surely this is the king of Israel!" Then they turned to fight against him. The robes did exactly what robes do.

He cries out, and that's all the text tells us he does. The chariot commanders are turning on him, and Jehoshaphat just hollers. I bet that was one loud, very sincere holler. Then the commanders see that he is not the king of Israel and turn back.

The text never has Jehoshaphat reach for a sword. It says, "Jehoshaphat cried out." Right after that, the commanders see he isn't the king of Israel and turn back from pursuing him. So the story moves on with a cry and no swordplay.

No robe-removal happens here. The text says Jehoshaphat cried out. Then the chariot commanders saw that he was not the king of Israel and turned back. Nothing in the passage says he changed his clothes.
Not quite. The text says the commanders "turned back from pursuing him." They had been chasing Jehoshaphat because they thought he was the king of Israel. Once they saw he wasn't, the chase was over.

False is right. When the chariot commanders saw that Jehoshaphat was not the king of Israel, they "turned back from pursuing him." Their order was about one king only, so the wrong man didn't interest them. Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, got to breathe again.

Yes, the king of Israel. A certain man draws his bow "without taking special aim," and the arrow strikes Ahab between the joints of his armor. Ahab went in disguised, and an arrow with no special aim still found him. This is a heavy turn in the story, so let's take it in quietly.

The king of Aram is the one who gave the order about the king of Israel, but he's not the one hit. The text says the arrow "struck the king of Israel between the joints of his armor." That's Ahab. The king of Aram isn't in the arrow's path at all.

The chariot commanders were looking for the king of Israel, and the arrow found him too. The text says the man's arrow "struck the king of Israel between the joints of his armor." Nobody is told the arrow hit a commander. It hit Ahab.
True. Ahab says to his charioteer, "Turn around and take me out of the battle, for I am badly wounded!" That's the king of Israel speaking, in his own words. I think this one hurts a little to read.

The text says he does ask. Ahab tells his charioteer, "Turn around and take me out of the battle, for I am badly wounded!" Those are his words after the arrow hits him. I think this part is heavy, so we'll let it be.

Evening is right. The text says Ahab was propped up in his chariot, facing the Arameans, and "that evening he died." It's a long day for everybody out there. This is a heavy moment, so we'll just say it plainly.

Morning is too early. The text says "The battle raged throughout that day," and Ahab was propped up in his chariot the whole time. Then "that evening he died." The day had gone a long way before it ended.

Noon doesn't fit. The battle raged throughout that day, and Ahab stayed propped up in his chariot facing the Arameans. It was "that evening" when he died. So the story runs well past the middle of the day.

True. As the sun was setting, a cry rang out in the army: "Every man to his own city, and every man to his own land!" The day's fighting is over, and the men are sent home. It's a fitting end to a very long day.

The text says the opposite. As the sun was setting, the cry rang out in the army: "Every man to his own city, and every man to his own land!" So the men are told to go home, not to stay and fight. The sunset and the cry arrive together.

explanations.answer: The word the LORD had spoken
explanations.explanation: That's it. The text says the dogs licked up Ahab's blood "according to the word that the LORD had spoken." So what happened at the pool of Samaria matches what the LORD said. When the LORD speaks, it stands.

explanations.answer: The curse a stranger had spoken
explanations.explanation: No stranger is mentioned here. The text says this happened "according to the word that the LORD had spoken." No curse is brought up in these verses. The word belongs to the LORD.

explanations.answer: The vow the elders had spoken
explanations.explanation: The elders don't come into this at all. The text says the dogs licked up Ahab's blood "according to the word that the LORD had spoken." It's the LORD's word that this lines up with. No vow is mentioned.

Yes, his son Ahaziah. The text says Ahab rested with his fathers, "and his son Ahaziah reigned in his place." So the crown stays in the family. And this is the last verse of the passage, so Ahab's story wraps up here.
Jehu isn't the name this passage gives. It says "his son Ahaziah reigned in his place." Ahaziah is Ahab's son, so he's the one who takes over. A king's son is the one named.

Obadiah isn't named in these verses at all. The text says Ahab rested with his fathers, "and his son Ahaziah reigned in his place." So the one who reigns after Ahab is his son. Ahaziah is the name to remember.
